This tutorial shows how to make interactive 'flow maps' with data from `{spanishoddata}` and the `{mapgl}` [@mapgl_r] data visualisation package, whose `add_flowmap()` function is powered by [Flowmap.gl](https://github.com/flowmap-gl/flowmap.gl). We cover two examples. [First](#simple-example), we only visualise the total flows for a single day. In the [second](#advanced-example) more advanced example we also use the time component that allows you to interactively filter flows by time of day. For both examples, make sure you first go though the initial [setup steps](#setup). To make static flow maps, please see the [static flow maps](https://ropenspain.github.io/spanishoddata/articles/flowmaps-static.html) tutorial.


## Setup {#setup}

Install the `{mapgl}` package (flow maps require version 0.5.2 or newer):

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("mapgl")
```

No access token or account is needed: in this tutorial we use the free [CARTO](https://carto.com/basemaps) dark basemap through `maplibre()`. If you prefer Mapbox basemaps, `add_flowmap()` works the same way on maps created with `mapboxgl()`, for which you will need a free Mapbox access token (see [account.mapbox.com/access-tokens/](https://account.mapbox.com/access-tokens/){target='_blank'}).


```{r}
library(spanishoddata)
library(mapgl)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
```

{{< include ../inst/vignette-include/setup-data-directory.qmd >}}

## Simple example - plot flows data as it is {#simple-example}

### Get data

#### Flows

Let us get the flows between `districts` for a tipycal working day `2021-04-07`:

```{r}
od_20210407 <- spod_get("od", zones = "distr", dates = "2021-04-07")

head(od_20210407)
```

#### Zones

We also get the district zones polygons to mathch the flows. We use version 1 for the polygons, because the selected date is in 2021, which corresponds to the v1 data (see the relevant [codebook](v1-2020-2021-mitma-data-codebook.qmd)).

```{r}
districts_v1 <- spod_get_zones("dist", ver = 1)

head(districts_v1)
```

### Prepare data for visualization

#### Expected data format

To visualise the flows, `add_flowmap()` expects two objects in the following format (we use the package's built-in data on bike sharing in Montréal for illustration; `bixi_locations` has `id`, `name`, `lat` and `lon` columns, and `bixi_flows` has `time`, `origin`, `dest` and `count` columns):

**Locations**

A `data.frame` with `id`, optional `name`, as well as `lat` and `lon` for coordinates of the locations in WGS84 (EPSG: 4326) coordinate reference system. Alternatively, you can provide an `sf` object with `POINT` geometries and an `id` column. It will be transformed to WGS84 automatically, which is what we do in this tutorial.

```{r}
str(mapgl::bixi_locations)
```


**Flows**

A `data.frame` with `origin`, `dest`, and `count` for the flows between locations, where `origin` and `dest` must match with `id`'s of the locations, and `count` is the number of trips between them. All `origin` and `dest` values must be present in the locations and there must be no missing values in these three columns. For temporal flow maps, there must also be a column with the timestamp (we will use `time`), as in the example below.

```{r}
str(mapgl::bixi_flows)
```



#### Aggregate data - count total flows

```{r}
od_20210407_total <- od_20210407 |>
  group_by(origin = id_origin, dest = id_destination) |>
  summarise(count = sum(n_trips, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> 
  collect()

head(od_20210407_total)
```

```

  <fct>    <fct>      <dbl>

2 01001_AM 01051    2508.

```

### Create locations table with coordinates {#create-locations-table}

We need the coordinates for each origin and destination. We can use the centroids of `districts_v1` polygons for that. We keep the zone `id` (it has to match the `origin` and `dest` of the flows) and use the names of the districts, so that they are shown when hovering over the locations on the map. There is no need to convert the coordinates to WGS84 manually, `add_flowmap()` does it for us.

```{r}
districts_v1_centroids <- districts_v1 |>
  st_centroid() |>
  mutate(name = coalesce(district_names_in_v2, id)) |>
  select(id, name)

head(districts_v1_centroids)
```


### Create the plot

Create the interactive flow map with the `add_flowmap()` function on top of a `maplibre()` basemap. In the example below we use a dark basemap, so we also set `flow_dark_mode = TRUE`, and we enable the `flow_clustering_enabled` option, which merges nearby locations when you zoom out. We do not recommend disabling the clustering when plotting the flows between hundreds and thousands of locations, as this will reduce the readability of the map.

```{r}
flowmap <- maplibre(
  style = carto_style("dark-matter"),
  center = c(-3.7, 40.4),
  zoom = 5,
  projection = "mercator"
) |>
  add_flowmap(
    id = "flows-2021-04-07",
    locations = districts_v1_centroids,
    flows = od_20210407_total,
    flow_dark_mode = TRUE,
    flow_clustering_enabled = TRUE,
    flow_lines_rendering_mode = "straight"
  )

flowmap
```

You can hover over the locations and flows to see the tooltips with the number of trips, and click on a location to filter the flows to and from it. See the `add_flowmap()` documentation for the full list of options, including the colour schemes (see `flowmap_color_schemes()`), tooltip and popup customisation, and the location filtering modes.

You can play around with the arguments of the `add_flowmap()` function. For example, you can turn on the animation by setting `flow_lines_rendering_mode = "animated-straight"` or draw curved flows with `flow_lines_rendering_mode = "curved"`:

```{r}
flowmap_anim <- maplibre(
  style = carto_style("dark-matter"),
  center = c(-3.7, 40.4),
  zoom = 5,
  projection = "mercator"
) |>
  add_flowmap(
    id = "flows-2021-04-07-animated",
    locations = districts_v1_centroids,
    flows = od_20210407_total,
    flow_dark_mode = TRUE,
    flow_clustering_enabled = TRUE,
    flow_lines_rendering_mode = "animated-straight"
  )

flowmap_anim
```

## Advanced example - time filter {#advanced-example}

After following the simple example, let us now add a time filter to the flows. We will use `add_flowmap()` together with `add_slider_control()` to plot flows between the districts around Barcelona for a typical working day `2021-04-07` and let the user select the time of day interactively.

### Prepare data for visualization

Just like before, we aggregate the data and rename some columns. This time we also keep the `date` and the `hour` (which corresponds to the hour of the day) and combine them into timestamps, so that the flows can be interactively filtered by time of day. We create the timestamps in the UTC time zone, so that the hours shown on the time slider are the same as the hours in the original data.

```{r}
od_20210407_time <- od_20210407 |>
  group_by(origin = id_origin, dest = id_destination, date, hour) |>
  summarise(count = sum(n_trips, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    time = as.POSIXct(date, tz = "UTC") + hour * 3600,
    origin = as.character(origin),
    dest = as.character(dest)
  ) |>
  select(origin, dest, time, count)

head(od_20210407_time)
```

### Filter the zones

Because we are now using the flows for each hour of the day, there are 24 times more rows in this data, than in the simple example. Therefore it will take longer to generate the plot and the resulting visualisation may work slower. To create a more manageable example, let us only filter the data to Barcelona and surrounding areas.

Let us select all districts that correspond to Barcelona and a 10 km radius around it. Thanks to the `district_names_in_v2` column in the zones data, we can easily select all the districts that correspond to Barcelona and then apply the spatial join on the to select some more districts around the polygons that correspond to Barcelona.

```{r}
zones_barcelona <- districts_v1 |>
  filter(grepl("Barcelona", district_names_in_v2, ignore.case = TRUE))

zones_barcelona_fua <- districts_v1[
  st_buffer(zones_barcelona, dist = 10000)
  ,
]

zones_barcelona_fua_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = zones_barcelona_fua, fill=NA, col = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  theme_minimal()

zones_barcelona_fua_plot
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ggsave("./man/figures/zones_barcelona_fua_plot.png", plot = zones_barcelona_fua_plot, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
```

![District zone boundaries in Barcelona and nearby areas](../man/figures/zones_barcelona_fua_plot.png){width=80%}

Now we prepare the table with locations for the flow map, just like in the simple example:

```{r}
zones_barcelona_fua_centroids <- zones_barcelona_fua |>
  st_centroid() |>
  mutate(name = coalesce(district_names_in_v2, id)) |>
  select(id, name)
```

### Prepare the flows

Now we can use the zone `id`s from the `zones_barcelona_fua` data to select the flows that correspond to Barcelona and the 10 km radius around it.

```{r}
od_20210407_time_barcelona <- od_20210407_time |>
  filter(origin %in% zones_barcelona_fua$id & dest %in% zones_barcelona_fua$id)
```

### Prepare the time slider

The time slider in `{mapgl}` works with numeric values, so we convert the timestamps to the number of seconds since 1970-01-01 with `as_time_property()`. We also count the total number of trips in each hour: this is used to draw a histogram, which you can brush with the mouse to select the time of day, and which helps to see the peaks of the mobility during the day.

```{r}
# all hours of the day
hours <- seq(
  min(od_20210407_time_barcelona$time),
  max(od_20210407_time_barcelona$time),
  by = "hour"
)

# total trips in each hour, including hours without any flows
trips_by_hour <- od_20210407_time_barcelona |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop")

hourly_counts <- trips_by_hour$count[match(hours, trips_by_hour$time)]
hourly_counts[is.na(hourly_counts)] <- 0

slider_values <- as_time_property(hours, unit = "seconds")
```

### Visualise the flows for Barcelona and surrounding areas

Now, we can create a new plot with this data. We tell `add_flowmap()` which column contains the time with `flow_time_column`, and then add a `"window"` mode slider control that targets the same layer `id`. With `presentation = "timeline"` the slider is shown as a brushable histogram of the hourly totals: drag the selected window along the timeline, or drag its edges to resize it. With the default `window_behavior`, the window can be resized freely, and initially covers the whole day.

```{r}
flowmap_time <- maplibre(
  style = carto_style("dark-matter"),
  bounds = zones_barcelona_fua,
  projection = "mercator"
) |>
  add_flowmap(
    id = "flows-barcelona",
    locations = zones_barcelona_fua_centroids,
    flows = od_20210407_time_barcelona,
    flow_time_column = "time",
    flow_dark_mode = TRUE,
    flow_clustering_enabled = TRUE
  ) |>
  add_slider_control(
    layers = "flows-barcelona",
    property = "time",
    time_unit = "seconds",
    values = slider_values,
    mode = "window",
    presentation = "timeline",
    counts = hourly_counts,
    position = "bottom-left",
    width = 400
  )

flowmap_time
```

To start with a narrower time window, for example the morning rush hour from 7:00 to 10:00, you can instead set `window = 3 * 3600` (the units are the same as in `values`, i.e. seconds) and `initial_value` to the end of the window: this gives a fixed width window that you can slide along the day.

```{r}
flowmap_time_morning <- maplibre(
  style = carto_style("dark-matter"),
  bounds = zones_barcelona_fua,
  projection = "mercator"
) |>
  add_flowmap(
    id = "flows-barcelona",
    locations = zones_barcelona_fua_centroids,
    flows = od_20210407_time_barcelona,
    flow_time_column = "time",
    flow_dark_mode = TRUE,
    flow_clustering_enabled = TRUE
  ) |>
  add_slider_control(
    layers = "flows-barcelona",
    property = "time",
    time_unit = "seconds",
    values = slider_values,
    mode = "window",
    window = 3 * 3600,
    initial_value = slider_values[hours == as.POSIXct("2021-04-07 10:00:00", tz = "UTC")],
    presentation = "timeline",
    counts = hourly_counts,
    position = "bottom-left",
    width = 400
  )

flowmap_time_morning
```
